chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: A quantum computer is a specialist tool, not just a faster laptop.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Quantum computers aren't here to replace your smartphone, make your internet browser faster, or run spreadsheets. Instead, they are highly specialized machines designed to solve specific types of problems that classical computers struggle with.
Where they won't help: Everyday computing tasks.

chunks.heading: Where they might help
chunks.text: Simulating quantum systems (like complex molecules for drug discovery or new battery materials), certain optimization and sampling problems, and specific cryptography tasks.

chunks.heading: The Secret Sauce
chunks.text: Quantum computers don't just "try every answer at once." They rely on superposition, entanglement, and above all interference (arranging amplitudes so wrong answers cancel out and right answers are amplified), followed by a final measurement.

chunks.heading: A common mix-up
chunks.text: A quantum computer does NOT try every answer at once.

chunks.heading: What a quantum computer is good for
chunks.text:
A quantum computer is a specialist machine. It is built to help with a short list of problem types, not to run everything faster.

The best-understood uses are: simulating quantum systems, such as molecules for drug discovery or new battery materials, because nature itself is quantum; some search, optimisation and sampling problems, where the speed-up is often modest or still being studied; and a few cryptography tasks. The famous example is Shor's algorithm, which could break the public-key encryption used on the web today, but only on a very large, error-corrected machine that does not exist yet.

For most of what a computer does, such as browsing, spreadsheets, video and games, a classical computer is better, cheaper and always will be.

chunks.heading: Why it is not just a faster laptop
chunks.text:
A classical computer follows one path through a calculation, step by step. A quantum computer does something different: it keeps a state described by amplitudes, shapes those amplitudes with gates, and uses interference so that wrong answers cancel out and right answers get stronger. Then it measures once and reads out one result.

That recipe only helps when a problem has the right structure for interference to exploit. That is why quantum computers give big speed-ups on a few problems and none on most.

chunks.heading: A spreadsheet versus a molecule
chunks.text:
Adding up a column of numbers in a spreadsheet gains nothing from quantum tricks: the answer is simple and a classical chip does it in microseconds.

Working out how a caffeine molecule behaves is different. The molecule's electrons follow quantum rules, and the number of possibilities to track grows extremely fast as the molecule gets bigger. A classical computer struggles to keep up, while a quantum computer follows the same rules natively. That is the kind of job people hope quantum computers will do well.

chunks.heading: Will a quantum computer replace my laptop or phone?
chunks.text: No. Quantum computers are not meant to replace everyday computers. They are specialised machines for certain problems, and they currently need extreme conditions such as very low temperatures or vacuum chambers. Think of one as a special tool that sits next to normal computers, not instead of them.

chunks.heading: Does a quantum computer try every answer at once?
chunks.text: No, this is the most common mix-up. A quantum computer does not just try all the answers in parallel and pick the right one. If it did, measuring would give a random answer out of all of them. The real power comes from interference: the algorithm arranges the amplitudes so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer is amplified before you measure. You will see this in Modules 4 and 6.

chunks.heading: Can a quantum computer break all encryption?
chunks.text: Not all of it, and not today. Shor's algorithm would break the public-key schemes (RSA and elliptic curves) that protect many websites, but it needs a large error-corrected quantum computer, far beyond today's machines. Everyday symmetric encryption such as AES is only weakened a little by quantum search, and can be protected by using longer keys. Researchers are also building "post-quantum" cryptography that quantum computers are not known to break.

chunks.heading: Are quantum computers real, or is it all hype?
chunks.text: They are real: there are working machines with tens to over a thousand physical qubits. But today's qubits are noisy and the machines are small, so clear, practical advantage over the best classical methods is still being demonstrated for useful problems. Be sceptical of headlines that promise instant revolutions; the field is promising but young.

chunks.heading: Key words from the orientation
chunks.text: A qubit is the quantum version of a bit. Superposition means a qubit's state is described by amplitudes for both 0 and 1. Entanglement is a link between qubits that cannot be described one at a time. Interference is the adding and cancelling of amplitudes, like waves. Measurement is reading out a result, which gives a plain 0 or 1. Quantum advantage means a quantum computer solving a task better than the best classical method.

chunks.heading: A quantum computer checks every answer at once
chunks.text: It sounds right and appears in many headlines, but it is not how quantum computers work. They do not read out all the answers. The gain comes from using interference to boost the right answer and cancel the wrong ones, followed by one measurement. If you remember one thing from this course, remember that.

chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: A qubit state is a point on a sphere, not "0 and 1 at the same time."

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Classical computers use bits, which are strictly 0 or 1. Quantum computers use qubits. A qubit's state is described by amplitudes over the outcomes 0 and 1.

chunks.heading: Superposition
chunks.text: When a qubit is in a superposition, it isn't "0 and 1 at the same time." Rather, it has a probability of being measured as 0, and a probability of being measured as 1.

chunks.heading: The Bloch Sphere
chunks.text: Imagine a 3D globe. The North Pole is the state |0⟩, and the South Pole is |1⟩. The equator represents equal-weight superpositions (like |+⟩ and |−⟩), where there is a 50/50 chance of measuring 0 or 1. A qubit's state is just a point on this sphere!

chunks.heading: A common mix-up
chunks.text: A qubit isn't "both at once."

chunks.heading: Bits, qubits and amplitudes
chunks.text:
A classical bit is always 0 or 1. A qubit's state is described by two numbers called amplitudes, one for the outcome 0 and one for the outcome 1. We write the state as α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where α and β are the amplitudes.

The amplitudes are not probabilities. The probability of measuring 0 is the square of the size of α, and the probability of measuring 1 is the square of the size of β. Because those two probabilities must add up to 100%, the amplitudes are linked: |α|² + |β|² = 1. That is called normalisation.

chunks.heading: What superposition really means
chunks.text:
When a qubit is in a superposition, it is described by amplitudes for both outcomes. It is not "secretly one of them, we just don't know which", and it is not simply "0 and 1 at the same time". A fair description is: it has a definite state that is a blend of |0⟩ and |1⟩, and when you measure it you get 0 or 1 with the probabilities the amplitudes give.

The blend itself is real and can be steered: later modules show amplitudes from different paths adding or cancelling, which probabilities for hidden values could never do.

chunks.heading: The Bloch sphere
chunks.text:
The Bloch sphere is a picture of one qubit's state as a point on a globe (this is a simplified model that works for a single qubit only). The North Pole is |0⟩ and the South Pole is |1⟩. The equator holds the equal blends, such as |+⟩ and |−⟩, where measuring gives 0 or 1 with 50% chance each.

How far north or south the point is tells you the probabilities of 0 and 1. How far around the globe it is (its longitude) is the relative phase between the two amplitudes, which does not change the 0/1 probabilities right away but matters later. For two or more qubits this simple globe no longer works, which is one reason entanglement is surprising.

chunks.heading: An equal superposition
chunks.text:
The state |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 has amplitude 1/√2 ≈ 0.71 for each outcome. Squaring gives 0.5, so measuring gives 0 half the time and 1 half the time. You make it by applying a Hadamard gate to |0⟩. On the Bloch sphere it sits on the equator.

A spinning coin is a common analogy: it is neither heads nor tails until it lands. This is only an analogy. A spinning coin really is heads or tails the whole time and we simply do not know which; a qubit in superposition is not hiding a pre-set answer.

chunks.heading: Is a qubit really 0 and 1 at the same time?
chunks.text: Not exactly. A qubit in superposition has amplitudes for both outcomes, which is why it behaves differently from a bit that is just unknown. But "0 and 1 at once" makes it sound like it stores two answers you could read out together. When you measure, you always get a single 0 or 1. The accurate statement is that its state is a blend, described by amplitudes, and the measurement result is random with the probabilities those amplitudes give.

chunks.heading: What is superposition?
chunks.text: Superposition means a quantum system's state is a combination of basis states, such as |0⟩ and |1⟩, each with an amplitude. Any state of a qubit that is not exactly |0⟩ or |1⟩ is a superposition of them.

chunks.heading: What is the Bloch sphere?
chunks.text: It is a way to draw the state of a single qubit as a point on a sphere. The poles are |0⟩ and |1⟩, the equator holds the 50/50 blends, and the angle around the sphere is the phase. It is a handy picture for one qubit, but it cannot show entangled states of several qubits.

chunks.heading: Why do we need amplitudes? Why not just probabilities?
chunks.text: Amplitudes can be negative or complex, so they can cancel each other, and probabilities cannot. That cancelling, called interference, is what makes quantum algorithms work. You will see it in Module 4.

chunks.heading: What is a qubit made of?
chunks.text: Different machines use different physical things: tiny superconducting circuits, single trapped ions, single atoms held by lasers, particles of light, or spins in silicon. Each choice has trade-offs. Part 2 of the course compares them.

chunks.heading: Key words
chunks.text: Qubit: the quantum version of a bit. Amplitude: a number (possibly negative or complex) attached to each outcome. Superposition: a state that is a combination of basis states. Basis states: the two reference states |0⟩ and |1⟩. Ket: the |...⟩ notation for a quantum state. Normalisation: the probabilities must add up to 1. Bloch sphere: a globe picture of one qubit.

chunks.heading: A qubit is both 0 and 1, so it stores infinite information
chunks.text: A qubit's state does take continuous values, but you cannot read them out. Measuring gives one bit, 0 or 1. One qubit never lets you extract more than one bit of information, however clever the blend was.

chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: One run is random; thousands of runs reveal the weights.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Measurement is the most aggressive action in quantum mechanics. When you measure a qubit in superposition, its state collapses to a single definite outcome (0 or 1).

chunks.heading: The Born Rule
chunks.text: The probability of an outcome is the squared magnitude of its amplitude.

chunks.heading: Shots & Histograms
chunks.text: Because one measurement gives a random result, quantum computers run the same circuit thousands of times (called "shots"). The results are plotted on a histogram to reveal the true probability weights.

chunks.heading: Measurement Bases
chunks.text: You can look at a qubit from different angles. Measuring in the standard (Z) basis checks if it's North or South. Measuring in the X basis checks the equator. A state that is 100% certain in one basis might be 50/50 random in another!

chunks.heading: A common mix-up
chunks.text: The value is not pre-determined. The act of measurement forces the qubit to choose.

chunks.heading: The Born rule and collapse
chunks.text:
When you measure a qubit you get 0 or 1, never a blend. The Born rule says the probability of each outcome is the squared size of its amplitude. For a state with amplitudes 0.6 for |0⟩ and 0.8 for |1⟩, the probabilities are 0.6² = 0.36 for 0 and 0.8² = 0.64 for 1. They add up to 1, as they must.

After the measurement, the qubit is in the state that matches the result. If you got 1, the qubit is now |1⟩, and measuring again gives 1 every time. This sudden change is called collapse. The maths of the Born rule is not disputed; what "really" happens during collapse is an interpretation question that physicists still discuss.

chunks.heading: Shots and histograms
chunks.text:
A single measurement is random, so one run tells you almost nothing about the amplitudes. Quantum computers therefore run the same circuit many times, often thousands. Each run is called a shot. Counting the results gives a histogram: a bar chart of how often each outcome appeared.

With more shots, the bars get closer to the true probabilities. The typical error shrinks like 1 divided by the square root of the number of shots, so 100 times more shots gives about 10 times less noise. With a true 50/50 state, 10 shots might give 3 zeros and 7 ones, while 10,000 shots will give something very close to 5,000 each.

chunks.heading: Measurement bases
chunks.text:
You can ask a qubit different questions. The usual question, the Z basis, asks "is it |0⟩ or |1⟩?" (North Pole or South Pole). Another question, the X basis, asks "is it |+⟩ or |−⟩?" (two points on the equator).

A state can be certain in one basis and random in another. The state |+⟩ gives a 50/50 random result in the Z basis, but gives "+" every time in the X basis. In practice you measure in the X basis by applying a Hadamard gate first and then measuring as usual.

chunks.heading: Ten shots versus a thousand
chunks.text: Take a qubit in |+⟩. Ten shots might show 0 four times and 1 six times. That does not mean the probability is 40/60; ten shots is too few to say. Run 1,000 shots and you might see 497 zeros and 503 ones, which points clearly to 50/50. Seeing a tiny gap from exactly 50/50 is normal statistical noise, not a sign of a broken qubit.

chunks.heading: Why is the measurement result random?
chunks.text: According to quantum mechanics, the randomness is built in. When the amplitudes are both non-zero, the outcome is not decided beforehand; the Born rule only gives the probabilities. Experiments such as the Bell tests in Module 5A rule out simple "hidden answer" explanations.

chunks.heading: What is wavefunction collapse?
chunks.text: It is the name for the sudden change when you measure: a superposition turns into one definite outcome. After it, the state matches what you measured. The rule for the probabilities (the Born rule) is well tested. What collapse means physically is debated, with several interpretations that make the same predictions.

chunks.heading: Does measurement need a conscious observer?
chunks.text: No. In physics, a measurement is any interaction that records the outcome in a way that cannot be undone, such as a detector clicking. No person has to look.

chunks.heading: Why do quantum computers run a circuit thousands of times?
chunks.text: Each run gives only one random 0 or 1 for each measured qubit. To see the probabilities, which carry the information, you repeat the run many times and count. These repeats are the shots, and the histogram is built from them.

chunks.heading: Can I measure a qubit without disturbing it?
chunks.text: Measuring a qubit in superposition changes its state to the result you got, so in general no. You can learn about an unknown state only by preparing it many times and measuring many copies, never by reading one copy fully.

chunks.heading: Key words
chunks.text: Measurement: reading out a qubit, giving 0 or 1. Born rule: probability equals the amplitude's size squared. Collapse: the state becoming the measured outcome. Shot: one run of a circuit. Histogram: counts of how often each result appeared. Basis: the question a measurement asks, such as Z or X.

chunks.heading: The value was already 0 or 1 before you looked
chunks.text: It is tempting to think the qubit secretly held a value and measurement just reveals it. For a state like |+⟩ there is no pre-set answer to reveal; the 50/50 result is created when you measure. The measurement forces the qubit to choose. (A qubit in |0⟩ is different: measuring it in the Z basis always gives 0.)

chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: H, Z, H in sequence equals X.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Classical computers use logic gates (AND, OR, NOT). Quantum computers use quantum gates, which are essentially rotations of the qubit's point around the Bloch sphere.
X Gate: A bit-flip (rotates North to South, like a classical NOT).
Reversibility: Every quantum gate can be undone by applying its inverse.

chunks.heading: Z Gate
chunks.text: A phase-flip (a half-turn around the vertical Z axis: |0⟩ and |1⟩ stay where they are, while |+⟩ swings around the equator to |−⟩).

chunks.heading: H Gate (Hadamard)
chunks.text: Moves a state from the poles to the equator (creates a superposition) and vice versa.

chunks.heading: Phase
chunks.text: Rotating around the equator changes a qubit's relative phase. This doesn't change the probability of measuring 0 or 1 right away, but it is the secret ingredient for interference.

chunks.heading: A common mix-up
chunks.text: People think Z "does nothing" because the probabilities don't change, but it changes the phase.

chunks.heading: Gates as rotations
chunks.text:
Classical gates (AND, OR, NOT) change bits. Quantum gates change a qubit's state, and on the Bloch sphere each one is a rotation of the state's point. Because a rotation never stretches or squashes anything, the probabilities always still add up to 1, and every gate can be undone by rotating back. Gates with this property are called unitary.

The main single-qubit gates are: X, a half-turn about the X axis that swaps North and South, so |0⟩ becomes |1⟩ and back (the quantum version of NOT); Z, a half-turn about the vertical axis that leaves |0⟩ and |1⟩ in place but swings |+⟩ round the equator to |−⟩; and H, the Hadamard gate, which moves a state between the poles and the equator.

chunks.heading: Phase
chunks.text:
A qubit state has a "relative phase": the sign or angle between its two amplitudes. On the Bloch sphere it is how far around the globe the point is. Changing the phase does not change the chance of measuring 0 or 1 right now, which is why a Z gate seems to do nothing if you measure straight after it.

But phase decides what happens next. If you apply an H gate after a Z, the phase turns into a different 0/1 probability. Phase is the hidden ingredient that makes interference possible in Module 4.

chunks.heading: Reversibility
chunks.text: Every quantum gate has an inverse that undoes it. X undoes itself (applying X twice does nothing), and so do H and Z. Reversibility is why you cannot "erase" a qubit with a gate, and why information is not lost until you measure.

chunks.heading: H, Z, H equals X
chunks.text: Start with |0⟩, North Pole. The first H moves it to |+⟩ on the equator. Z swings it around the equator to |−⟩. The second H moves |−⟩ down to the South Pole, |1⟩. Overall |0⟩ became |1⟩, which is exactly what an X gate does. This works for any starting state: H followed by Z followed by H always acts exactly like X.

chunks.heading: Does the Z gate do nothing?
chunks.text: It does not do nothing, but you may not see it with a quick measurement. Z flips the sign of the |1⟩ amplitude. If you measure right away, the probabilities of 0 and 1 are the same as before. But the phase has changed, and a following H gate turns that into a visible difference.

chunks.heading: What does the Hadamard (H) gate do?
chunks.text: It moves a qubit between the poles and the equator. Applied to |0⟩ it gives |+⟩, an equal blend of 0 and 1. Applied to |+⟩ it gives |0⟩ back. It is the most common gate for making a superposition.

chunks.heading: How is the X gate different from a classical NOT?
chunks.text: On |0⟩ and |1⟩ they do the same thing. The difference is that X also works on superpositions: it swaps the two amplitudes, so α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ becomes β|0⟩ + α|1⟩. A classical NOT can only handle a definite 0 or 1.

chunks.heading: Why must quantum gates be reversible?
chunks.text: Quantum mechanics keeps total probability equal to 1 and describes closed systems with reversible transformations. The only irreversible step is measurement. For this reason every gate is unitary and has an inverse.

chunks.heading: Are there more gates than X, Z and H?
chunks.text: Yes. Any rotation of the Bloch sphere is a valid single-qubit gate. Real machines support a small basic set from which others are built, and in Module 5A you will meet the CNOT, a gate that acts on two qubits.

chunks.heading: Key words
chunks.text: Gate: an operation on qubits. Unitary: a reversible, probability-preserving transformation. X, Y, Z: the Pauli gates, half-turns about each axis. H (Hadamard): moves between poles and equator. Phase: the relative angle between the two amplitudes. Inverse: the gate that undoes another.

chunks.heading: Z does nothing because the probabilities don't change
chunks.text: Z changes the phase, and phase changes the outcome of later gates. It is invisible to an immediate measurement but not to the rest of the circuit. H, Z, H acting as X shows it clearly.

chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: A "guaranteed" path can go dark due to cancellation.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
This is where quantum computing gets its power. Because quantum states are described by amplitudes (which can be positive, negative, or complex numbers), they can add together like waves.
Constructive Interference: Amplitudes with the same sign add up, making an outcome more likely.

chunks.heading: Destructive Interference
chunks.text: Amplitudes with opposite signs cancel each other out, making an outcome less likely, or completely impossible when they cancel exactly.

chunks.heading: The Mach-Zehnder Interferometer
chunks.text: If you split a photon's path (putting it in superposition), change its phase, and recombine it, you can direct 100% of the photon to a specific detector. If you block one path, the interference is destroyed, and the photons that get through reach either detector with 50/50 odds.

chunks.heading: A common mix-up
chunks.text: Probabilities don't just add up. Amplitudes add up first.

chunks.heading: Amplitudes add before you square
chunks.text:
In everyday probability, if there are two ways to reach an outcome, you add their probabilities. Quantum mechanics adds the amplitudes first, and only then squares the result to get a probability. Amplitudes can be positive or negative, so they can cancel. That cancelling is destructive interference. When they have the same sign they reinforce each other, which is constructive interference.

This is the central trick of quantum computing: arrange the circuit so that the paths to wrong answers cancel and the paths to the right answer add up.

chunks.heading: The Mach-Zehnder interferometer
chunks.text:
This is a setup with one photon, two beam splitters and two detectors. The first beam splitter puts the photon into a superposition of two paths. A phase shifter can change the relative phase of one path. The second beam splitter recombines the paths.

With equal paths, the contributions to one detector add and to the other cancel, so the photon always reaches the same detector, 100% of the time. Changing the phase by half a wavelength swaps which detector gets it. If you block one path, interference is destroyed: only the photons that took the other path get through, and those reach each detector with 50/50 odds. That is the surprise of the setup: removing one of the two routes makes the previously dark detector light up.

chunks.heading: H then H gives back |0⟩
chunks.text: Start with |0⟩. After the first H, the amplitudes are 1/√2 for |0⟩ and 1/√2 for |1⟩. Apply H again. The amplitude for ending at |1⟩ has two routes: through |0⟩ with +1/√2 × 1/√2 = +1/2, and through |1⟩ with −1/2. They cancel to 0. For ending at |0⟩ the two routes give +1/2 and +1/2, adding to 1. So the second H returns the qubit to |0⟩ with certainty. Adding probabilities, 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, would wrongly predict a coin flip.

chunks.heading: What is interference?
chunks.text: It is what happens when the amplitudes for different routes to the same outcome combine. Like water waves, they can reinforce or cancel. The size of the combined amplitude, squared, is the probability.

chunks.heading: What is the difference between constructive and destructive interference?
chunks.text: Constructive means the amplitudes have the same sign and add up, making the outcome more likely. Destructive means opposite signs, so they cancel and make the outcome less likely, or impossible if they cancel exactly.

chunks.heading: Why can't I just add the probabilities?
chunks.text: Because the probabilities hide the signs. Two routes with probability 1/4 each can give 1 or 0 for the outcome, depending on whether their amplitudes add or cancel. Only by adding amplitudes first can you get this right, and experiments confirm it.

chunks.heading: Is the photon really in both paths at once?
chunks.text: "Both paths" is loose language. Its state is a superposition of the two path states, and the amplitudes for both routes take part in the result. If you put a detector in a path to see which way it went, you find it in only one, and the interference vanishes.

chunks.heading: Is interference how quantum computers get speed-ups?
chunks.text: Yes. Algorithms such as Deutsch-Jozsa and Grover in Module 6 are designed so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer is boosted.

chunks.heading: Key words
chunks.text: Interference: amplitudes combining like waves. Constructive: amplitudes add. Destructive: amplitudes cancel. Phase: the angle that decides whether amplitudes add or cancel. Beam splitter: a half-silvered mirror that puts a photon into a superposition of two paths. Interferometer: a device that recombines split paths.

chunks.heading: Probabilities just add up
chunks.text: For quantum events with several routes, amplitudes add first and probabilities come from squaring the total. That is why a "guaranteed" path can go dark: the amplitudes cancel.

chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: Correlations that no classical strategy can match.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: When two qubits interact (using a two-qubit gate like a CNOT), their states can become linked. This is entanglement.

chunks.heading: Exponential Space
chunks.text: 1 qubit has 2 amplitudes. 2 qubits have 4. 10 qubits have 1024. The state space doubles with every added qubit!

chunks.heading: Correlations
chunks.text: Measuring one entangled qubit instantly tells you the state of the other, no matter how far apart they are. But each individual result is still random, so this cannot be used to send a message.

chunks.heading: Bell's Inequality & CHSH
chunks.text: Einstein suspected the correlations came from hidden classical instructions ("local hidden variables"). The CHSH game tests this: any classical strategy wins at most 75% of the time, while players sharing entanglement can reach about 85% (cos²(π/8) ≈ 85.4%). Real experiments, recognized by the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics, beat the classical limit.

chunks.heading: A common mix-up
chunks.text: You cannot use entanglement to send an instant text message.

chunks.heading: Making an entangled pair
chunks.text:
Entanglement is a link between qubits that cannot be described one at a time. A standard way to make it: start two qubits in |00⟩, apply an H gate to the first one to make it a superposition, then apply a CNOT gate, which flips the second qubit only if the first one is 1. The result is the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.

In that state there is no separate state for each qubit. Measuring either one gives 0 or 1 at random, 50% each. But the two results always agree: both 0 or both 1. The pair as a whole is well defined, while the individual qubits are not.

chunks.heading: Why you cannot send a message with entanglement
chunks.text: Each person's result, taken alone, is a fair coin flip. What entanglement gives is a link between the two results, and you can only see that link when the two people compare their results, which needs a normal message sent at ordinary speed. Whatever Alice does to her qubit, Bob's results alone still look random. This is why entanglement cannot be used to send information faster than light. It does not violate relativity.

chunks.heading: Bell's inequality and the CHSH game
chunks.text: Einstein suspected the correlations came from hidden instructions set when the pair was created, like two sealed boxes with matching tickets. John Bell showed how to test this. In the CHSH game, Alice and Bob each get a random bit and each answer with one bit, without talking. They win if the XOR of their two answers equals the AND of their two input bits. Any strategy built on pre-agreed hidden instructions wins at most 75% of the time. Players sharing an entangled pair and measuring in cleverly chosen directions win about 85.4% of the time (cos²(π/8)). Real experiments, including loophole-free ones, find results above 75%, ruling out local hidden variables. The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured this work.

chunks.heading: Exponential space
chunks.text: One qubit needs 2 amplitudes. Two qubits need 4, three need 8, and 10 qubits need 1,024. The description doubles with every qubit added. This is why simulating many qubits on a classical computer gets hard fast. But it does not by itself make quantum computers faster: a measurement of n qubits still returns just n bits.

chunks.heading: Two gloves in sealed boxes
chunks.text: Put a left and a right glove in two sealed boxes and send them to opposite sides of the world. Opening one box instantly tells you what the other holds. That is a classical correlation, and nothing travels between the boxes. This is an analogy that captures part of it, but Bell's theorem shows entanglement is stronger than this: no pre-set contents can reproduce all the quantum results.

chunks.heading: Can entanglement send messages faster than light?
chunks.text: No. Each side's results look random on their own. The pattern only shows up when the results are compared by ordinary communication, so no information travels faster than light.

chunks.heading: What is a Bell state?
chunks.text: A Bell state is one of four maximally entangled two-qubit states. The most common is (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, made with an H gate and a CNOT. Measuring both qubits always gives matching results.

chunks.heading: What did Einstein mean by "spooky action at a distance"?
chunks.text: He was uneasy that measuring one half of an entangled pair seems to settle the result of the other half instantly. He thought hidden properties must explain it. Bell's theorem and experiments show that no local hidden-variable theory can match the quantum predictions.

chunks.heading: Is entanglement just correlation?
chunks.text: Ordinary correlation, like the gloves, can be explained by pre-set values. Entanglement gives correlations that no pre-set values can reproduce, which the CHSH game shows (more than 75% wins).

chunks.heading: How do you entangle two qubits?
chunks.text: Use a two-qubit gate such as CNOT after putting one qubit into a superposition. In the Two-Qubit Lab you can build the Bell state and see the correlations.

chunks.heading: Key words
chunks.text: Entanglement: a link between qubits that cannot be described separately. CNOT: a two-qubit gate that flips the second qubit if the first is 1. Bell state: a maximally entangled two-qubit state. Local hidden variables: the idea that results are set in advance. CHSH: a game that tests Bell's inequality. Correlation: how often results agree.

chunks.heading: Entanglement lets you send an instant text message
chunks.text: Measuring one qubit does not let you control the other's result, and on its own Bob's result is random. Nothing usable is sent until Alice tells Bob her result by normal means.

chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: You can move a quantum state without copying it.

chunks.heading: No-Cloning Theorem
chunks.text: It is physically impossible to make an exact copy of an unknown quantum state. If you try to measure it to copy it, you destroy the superposition.

chunks.heading: Quantum Teleportation
chunks.text: How do we move a qubit if we can't copy it? Teleportation! By consuming a shared pair of entangled qubits and sending two classical bits of information, Alice can destroy a quantum state on her end and make it perfectly reconstruct on Bob's end. Bob cannot recover the state until the two classical bits arrive, so teleportation is never faster than light.

chunks.heading: Why you cannot copy a qubit
chunks.text:
The no-cloning theorem says there is no way to make an exact copy of an unknown quantum state. A short reason: copying would have to work for every state, but quantum operations are linear, and a linear copier that works for |0⟩ and |1⟩ gives the wrong answer for blends of them. Measuring first to learn the state does not help either, because the measurement destroys the superposition and gives only 0 or 1.

You can copy classical bits, and you can build a copy of a state if you already know how it was prepared. What you cannot do is copy a state you do not know.

chunks.heading: How teleportation works
chunks.text:
Teleportation moves a qubit's state from Alice to Bob without sending the qubit. They first share an entangled pair, one half each. Alice has the qubit to send. She makes a joint measurement of her qubit and her half of the pair (a CNOT, then an H, then measuring both). This gives two ordinary bits and destroys the original state. She sends those two bits to Bob by normal means.

Bob's half of the pair is now in one of four possible states related to the original. Depending on the two bits, he applies nothing, an X gate, a Z gate, or both. After that his qubit is exactly the state Alice started with.

chunks.heading: Why it is not faster than light, and why the state is not copied
chunks.text: Until the two classical bits arrive, Bob's qubit looks completely random; each of the four possible bit pairs is equally likely (25% each), so without the bits he has nothing useful. The bits travel at no more than the speed of light, so teleportation cannot beat it. The state is also not copied: Alice's measurement destroys her version, so there is only ever one copy. Teleportation moves the state, it does not move matter, and it uses up the shared entangled pair.

chunks.heading: Alice sends a mystery qubit
chunks.text: Alice wants to send a qubit in a state neither she nor Bob knows. She measures, gets bits 1 and 0, and sends them. Bob sees "1, 0", so he applies the matching correction. His qubit now equals the original. If the bits had been 0 and 0, he would have done nothing. In the Teleportation Lab you can step through this and see Bob's fidelity (how close his qubit is to the original) jump to 100% only after the correction.

chunks.heading: Why can't we just copy the qubit?
chunks.text: Because of the no-cloning theorem: no machine can copy an unknown quantum state exactly. This also keeps quantum cryptography secure, since an eavesdropper cannot make a perfect copy.

chunks.heading: Why does teleportation need two classical bits?
chunks.text: Alice's joint measurement has four possible results, which take two bits to name. Bob needs to know which one happened to pick the right correction (nothing, X, Z, or both).

chunks.heading: Does teleportation move the actual particle?
chunks.text: No. It moves the state, not the matter. Bob's qubit is a different physical qubit that ends up in the state Alice's qubit had.

chunks.heading: Can teleportation send information faster than light?
chunks.text: No. The correction needs the two classical bits, and they travel at the normal speed of communication.

chunks.heading: What is teleportation used for?
chunks.text: It is used in quantum networks and in some proposals for connecting quantum computers, and as a building block in fault-tolerant computing, where it moves states and performs certain gates safely.

chunks.heading: Key words
chunks.text: No-cloning theorem: unknown quantum states cannot be copied. Teleportation: moving a quantum state using entanglement and two classical bits. Bell measurement: Alice's joint measurement of her two qubits. Correction: the X and/or Z gates Bob applies. Fidelity: how close two states are (100% means identical).

chunks.heading: Teleportation is like in science fiction
chunks.text: Nothing physical is sent, nothing is instant, and the original is not left behind. It is a careful way to move a quantum state using entanglement and a normal message.

chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: Algorithms arrange interference so wrong answers cancel.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Oracles: Think of an oracle as a "black box" puzzle.

chunks.heading: Reading Circuits
chunks.text: Quantum circuits are read left to right. Lines are qubits, boxes are gates.

chunks.heading: Deutsch-Jozsa
chunks.text: Proves that a quantum computer can solve a specific puzzle (is a hidden function constant or balanced?) in exactly one query using interference, while a deterministic classical computer may need up to 2ⁿ⁻¹ + 1 queries in the worst case.

chunks.heading: Grover's Algorithm
chunks.text: Used for searching. It uses "amplitude amplification"—the oracle flips the sign of the right answer's amplitude, then a diffusion step (a reflection about the average) amplifies it. Repeating this about (π/4)√N times makes the right answer the most probable outcome.

chunks.heading: Reading a circuit and what an oracle is
chunks.text:
A quantum circuit is read from left to right. Each horizontal line is a qubit, each box is a gate, and a meter symbol at the end is a measurement. The qubits usually start in |0⟩.

An oracle is a black box: a gate that stands for a function whose inner workings you cannot see. You can only use the box and see what it does. Many quantum algorithms are described in terms of how many times they need to use the oracle, called queries, because that gives a clean way to compare quantum and classical methods.

chunks.heading: The Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm
chunks.text:
The puzzle: a hidden function takes n bits and returns 0 or 1. You are promised it is either constant (the same answer for every input) or balanced (0 for exactly half the inputs, 1 for the other half). Which is it?

A classical computer that always gives the right answer may need up to 2^(n−1) + 1 queries in the worst case. The quantum circuit uses the oracle once: put the input qubits in an equal superposition with H gates, call the oracle, apply H again and measure. If every input qubit reads 0, the function is constant; otherwise it is balanced. Interference makes the "all zeros" outcome certain for constant functions and impossible for balanced ones.

This is a toy problem. A randomised classical algorithm can answer it with only a few queries and a tiny chance of error, so the speed-up is relative to a deterministic classical method. Its value is as the first clear example of a quantum advantage and as the inspiration for later algorithms.

chunks.heading: Grover's search
chunks.text:
Grover's algorithm searches an unsorted list of N items for the one marked item. A classical search checks about N/2 items on average. Grover needs about (π/4)√N steps, which is a quadratic speed-up, much less dramatic than exponential.

Each step has two parts. First the oracle flips the sign of the marked item's amplitude. Then the diffusion step reflects every amplitude about their average, which makes the marked amplitude bigger and the others smaller. Repeating rotates the state steadily toward the answer. It is a rotation, so you must stop at the right time: doing too many steps rotates past the answer and the success chance falls again.

chunks.heading: Grover on 4 items, by hand
chunks.text: With 2 qubits there are N = 4 items. After H gates, each has amplitude 1/2. The oracle flips the marked one to −1/2. The average of the four amplitudes is (3 × 1/2 − 1/2) / 4 = 1/4. Reflecting about the average maps each amplitude a to 2 × 1/4 − a. For the three unmarked items that gives 1/2 → 0, and for the marked item −1/2 → 1. After a single step, the marked item has probability 100%. For larger N you need more steps and the success chance gets close to, but not exactly, 100%.

chunks.heading: Is Grover's algorithm exponentially faster?
chunks.text: No. It is quadratically faster: about √N steps instead of about N. That is useful for huge searches but not a miracle.

chunks.heading: What is an oracle?
chunks.text: A black-box function you can run but not look inside. It is how algorithm analysts count the cost: by the number of times they call it.

chunks.heading: Why does Grover need about the square root of N steps?
chunks.text: Each step rotates the state by a small, fixed angle toward the marked item, an angle of about 2/√N. You need about (π/4)√N such rotations to turn the state from "evenly spread" to "pointing at the answer".

chunks.heading: What happens if I run too many Grover steps?
chunks.text: The state keeps rotating past the answer, so the success probability falls again. The Grover Explorer lets you see this.

chunks.heading: Does the quantum computer check all the items at once?
chunks.text: No. The oracle is used on a superposition, but you cannot read out all the results. Interference over several steps is what concentrates the probability on the right answer.

chunks.heading: Key words
chunks.text: Circuit: gates in time order. Oracle: a black-box function. Query: one use of the oracle. Constant and balanced: the two kinds of function in Deutsch-Jozsa. Amplitude amplification: boosting the right answer's amplitude. Diffusion: reflection about the average amplitude.

chunks.heading: Quantum algorithms try every answer at once
chunks.text: They use an oracle on a superposition, but the key work is done by interference, which cancels wrong answers and strengthens the right one. Without that, measuring would just give a random item.

chunks.heading: The key idea
chunks.text: You can find an error without looking at the data.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Physical qubits are fragile. Heat, radiation, and vibrations cause decoherence (losing their quantum state) and errors (unwanted bit-flips or phase-flips).
Since we can't copy qubits (No-Cloning), how do we do error correction?

chunks.heading: Parity Checks
chunks.text: We use extra qubits (ancilla qubits) to check the relationship between data qubits without actually measuring the data itself. Measuring the ancillas gives an error "syndrome" that shows which qubit flipped, without revealing the encoded information.

chunks.heading: Logical Qubits
chunks.text: By grouping many noisy "physical" qubits together with error correction codes, we create one far more reliable "logical" qubit. In the 3-qubit repetition code, if each qubit flips with probability p, the logical error rate is 3p² − 2p³, which is smaller than p whenever p is below 50%.

chunks.heading: A common mix-up
chunks.text: Measuring the data directly ruins the quantum state.

chunks.heading: Why qubits make mistakes
chunks.text:
Physical qubits are delicate. Heat, stray radiation, vibration and imperfect control pulses disturb them. Decoherence is the loss of the quantum state as the qubit gets tangled up with its surroundings. There are two main error types: a bit-flip (the effect of an X gate, swapping 0 and 1) and a phase-flip (the effect of a Z gate, changing the relative phase). Real errors can be any mixture.

Today's best machines make roughly one error in every hundred to few thousand two-qubit gates, far too many for long algorithms. That is why error correction matters.

chunks.heading: Encoding without copying
chunks.text: You cannot copy a qubit because of the no-cloning theorem, so error correction does not store three copies. Instead, it spreads the state across several qubits using entanglement. In the three-qubit bit-flip code, α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ becomes α|000⟩ + β|111⟩. That is not three copies of the state; it is a single entangled state.

chunks.heading: Parity checks and the syndrome
chunks.text: To find an error without looking at the data, add extra "ancilla" qubits and use them to compare pairs of data qubits: do qubits 1 and 2 agree? Do 2 and 3 agree? Measuring only the ancillas gives a pattern called the syndrome. If one data qubit flipped, the pattern tells you which one, and you flip it back. The ancilla measurements reveal only whether qubits agree, not whether they are 0 or 1, so the encoded information (α and β) is untouched.

chunks.heading: Logical qubits
chunks.text: A group of noisy physical qubits protected by a code acts as one more reliable logical qubit. In the three-qubit code, if each physical qubit flips with probability p, the logical error rate is 3p² − 2p³. For p = 0.1 that is 0.03 − 0.002 = 0.028, much better than 0.1. This only helps when p is below a threshold; with p above 50% it would make things worse. This simple code only handles bit-flips. Real codes, such as the surface code, handle both kinds and may need hundreds to thousands of physical qubits for each logical qubit.

chunks.heading: The syndrome table
chunks.text: For the three-qubit code, the two checks give a pattern. Both checks fine means no error. Check 1 (qubits 1 and 2) fails but check 2 is fine means qubit 1 flipped. Both fail means qubit 2 flipped. Only check 2 (qubits 2 and 3) fails means qubit 3 flipped. Each case has its own fix. The rule looks at which pair disagrees, never at the values themselves.

chunks.heading: Why can't we just make backup copies of a qubit?
chunks.text: Because the no-cloning theorem forbids copying an unknown state. Error correction uses entangled encoding and parity checks instead.

chunks.heading: What is decoherence?
chunks.text: Decoherence is the loss of a qubit's quantum behaviour as it interacts with its environment. It sets how long a qubit stays useful, called its coherence time.

chunks.heading: Why measure the ancillas but not the data?
chunks.text: Measuring the data qubits would collapse the superposition and destroy the information. Measuring the ancillas tells you only which qubits disagree, which reveals the error and not the data.

chunks.heading: How many physical qubits make one logical qubit?
chunks.text: It depends on the code and the error rate. Estimates for useful machines range from a few hundred to many thousands per logical qubit.

chunks.heading: What is the difference between error mitigation and error correction?
chunks.text: Error mitigation reduces the effect of noise by running extra experiments and processing the results afterwards. It does not protect the qubits. Error correction encodes the information so errors can be detected and fixed while the computation runs, and is needed for large algorithms.

chunks.heading: Key words
chunks.text: Decoherence: loss of the quantum state to the environment. Bit-flip and phase-flip: the two basic error types. Ancilla: an extra helper qubit. Syndrome: the pattern of parity check results. Physical qubit and logical qubit: the real noisy qubit and the protected one built from many. Threshold: the error rate below which correction helps.

chunks.heading: To check for errors you must measure the data
chunks.text: Measuring the data qubits ruins the superposition. Parity checks on ancillas find errors without learning the encoded state.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
All hardware metrics (qubit counts, fidelity) represent the current landscape and are subject to rapid change. Every physical modality represents a different engineering trade-off.
To build a quantum computer, we need a budget.
Gate Speed & Fidelity: How fast we can do operations, and how accurately.

chunks.heading: T1 & T2 Times
chunks.text: T1 is how long a qubit holds its energy before relaxing from |1⟩ to |0⟩; T2 is how long it keeps a stable phase (its superposition). Together they set the coherence time.

chunks.heading: The Budget
chunks.text: The number of operations you can do is roughly the coherence time divided by the gate time. For example, T2 = 100 µs with 50 ns gates gives a budget of about 2,000 operations, and fewer once gate errors are counted.

chunks.text: Who uses them: IBM, Google, Rigetti.

chunks.heading: How they work
chunks.text: Microchips made of superconducting metals (like niobium) cooled to near absolute zero (10-20 millikelvin) in giant dilution refrigerators. They are controlled by microwave pulses.

chunks.heading: Trade-offs
chunks.text: Very fast gates, but highly susceptible to noise. The cryogenics are a massive scaling bottleneck.

chunks.heading: How they work
chunks.text: Individual charged atoms (ions) suspended in a vacuum by electromagnetic fields, controlled by precision lasers.

chunks.heading: Trade-offs
chunks.text: Incredible coherence times and all-to-all connectivity within a chain (any ion can interact directly with any other ion in the same trap), but gate speeds are slower than superconducting, and scaling beyond one chain requires shuttling ions or linking separate traps.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Who uses them: QuEra, Pasqal, Atom Computing.

chunks.heading: How they work
chunks.text: Uncharged atoms gripped by optical tweezers (lasers). Lasers excite them to high-energy Rydberg states; when two atoms are close, an excited atom blocks its neighbor from being excited (the "Rydberg blockade"), which is used to build entangling gates.

chunks.heading: Trade-offs
chunks.text: Can pack massive amounts of qubits into tiny arrays, but controlling them accurately at scale is an ongoing physics challenge.

How they work: Information is stored in properties of light (photons) traveling through waveguides.

chunks.heading: Trade-offs
chunks.text: The waveguides and routing can operate near room temperature (though detectors often need cooling). The main enemy is loss (photons escaping or being absorbed) and the probabilistic nature of photon interactions.

chunks.text: Storing quantum information in the spin of a single electron trapped in a quantum dot on a silicon chip.

chunks.heading: Trade-offs
chunks.text: Massive scaling potential because they can be manufactured using existing global semiconductor fab infrastructure. However, tuning millions of microscopic dots perfectly is incredibly difficult.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Who uses them: D-Wave.

chunks.heading: How they work
chunks.text: Not a "universal" gate-model computer. Instead, you map an optimization problem into a physical energy landscape, let it cool down (anneal), and the system settles into the lowest energy state (the answer).

chunks.heading: Trade-offs
chunks.text: Great for specific optimization problems, but cannot run general algorithms like Shor's or Grover's. Whether annealers beat the best classical methods on real problems is still debated.

chunks.heading: Topological qubits
chunks.text: Store information in collective properties of exotic materials, so local noise should not easily disturb it. Microsoft is pursuing this approach; early experimental claims are still debated by physicists.

chunks.heading: Cat (bosonic) qubits
chunks.text: Encode a qubit in states of a microwave resonator that naturally resist bit-flips, so less error correction is needed (explored by AWS and the startup Alice & Bob).

chunks.text: Link several smaller quantum processors with photons, instead of building one giant chip.

Vectors: A list of numbers. Quantum states are column vectors.
Matrices: Grids of numbers used to multiply and transform vectors.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The state |0⟩ is written as the vector: |0⟩ = column (1, 0)
The state |1⟩ is written as the vector: |1⟩ = column (0, 1)
A superposition |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ is written as: |ψ⟩ = column (α, β)

chunks.heading: Rule
chunks.text: To conserve 100% probability, the amplitudes must satisfy (Normalization): |α|² + |β|² = 1

Quantum gates are Unitary Matrices. When a gate acts on a qubit, you multiply the matrix by the state vector.

To combine qubits, we use the Tensor Product.
Two qubits mean a vector of 4 amplitudes, one for each of these basis states: |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩
A 2-qubit gate like CNOT is a 4x4 matrix.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The Mach-Zehnder interferometer is represented mathematically as: H · Phase · H
If you multiply these matrices, you will see mathematically how the negative components of the matrix cancel out specific amplitudes (destructive interference), proving why one detector goes dark.

Grover's algorithm is just geometry! The Oracle is a reflection matrix (flipping the sign of the target state). The Diffusion operator is a reflection around the average.
Optimal iterations: Roughly the following, where N is the number of items: π/4√N
